title: DfE Decoded #154 Whether You Like PISA or Not, People Will Use It
author: Urry, Paul
summary: This piece walks school leaders through England's PISA 2025 results with a deliberate emphasis on nuance over headline rankings, arguing that whether or not one trusts international assessments, they will shape policy and media narratives regardless, so leaders need to understand what the data actually shows. England scored significantly above OECD averages in all three domains, with science showing genuine improvement, reading showing stability while other countries declined, and mathematics essentially flat but masking a widening gap between the highest and lowest performers. The piece surfaces findings that complicate simple narratives: a widening mathematics and science gender gap favoring boys (26 points in math, up from 12 in 2015), a large and persistent socioeconomic attainment gap, yet a meaningful cohort of 'academically resilient' disadvantaged pupils who outperform expectations, and second-generation immigrant pupils outperforming non-immigrant pupils in both reading and math. The author closes by cautioning against overreacting to any single headline figure, arguing the more useful question for school leaders is not 'where did England finish?' but 'what is happening underneath the average — and what might that tell us about the children our education system is serving?'
points: England scored significantly above OECD averages in all three PISA 2025 domains: 516 in science (up from 503 in 2022), 497 in reading, and 492 in mathematics.
A significant and widening gender gap favors boys in mathematics (26 points, up from 12 in 2015) and has newly emerged in science (13 points, versus effectively none in 2015).

The socioeconomic attainment gap remains large and stable (81-89 points across domains), but 13-16% of the most disadvantaged pupils are identified as 'academically resilient,' performing in the top quarter despite disadvantage.
Second-generation immigrant pupils significantly outperformed non-immigrant pupils in reading and mathematics, complicating simpler narratives about immigration and educational attainment.

The results are explicitly caveated as coming from a sample of 5,619 pupils in 183 schools, not a full census, with non-participating pupils skewing toward FSM-eligible and SEN populations — meaning trends should be read cautiously.
quotes: England's 15-year-olds scored: 516 in science, compared with an OECD average of 482. 497 in reading, compared with 461. 492 in mathematics, compared with 463. All three differences are statistically significant.
Girls scored 478. Boys scored 504. That's a 26-point gap. In 2015 the gap was 12 points.
The difference between the most and least disadvantaged quarters of pupils in England was: 81 points in science. 66 points in reading. 89 points in mathematics.
In England, that applies to: 14% in science. 16% in reading. 13% in mathematics... Socioeconomic circumstances are strongly associated with attainment. But they don't determine it.
In reading, second-generation pupils scored 515, compared with 504 for non-immigrant pupils. In mathematics, it was 511 compared with 497.
Whether we like PISA or not... these results will influence the conversation about education. They'll influence policy. They'll appear in speeches.
